deep.reconstruction:
This page has no mathematics. It is a short reading note, headed 'Physikalische Notizen'. In it Riemann summarizes a report in the journal L'Institut, no. 1133 (19 Sept. 1855). The report concerns Léon Foucault's communication to the Académie des sciences at the session of 17 Sept. 1855. A right-column heading reads roughly 'Wärmewirkungen magnetelektrischer Ströme in ...' ('Heat effects of magneto-electric currents in ...', the last word uncertain).

Content, in paraphrase: a solid bronze body was spun at 150–200 revolutions per second by a gear train. Riemann first wrote a German word for it, then 'tore', struck that out, and copied Foucault's 'un tore en bronze'. The body sat on a hardened shaft that forms its extension or axis. While spinning it was exposed to the poles of a strong electromagnet. A thermometer inserted into its mass rose from 16 °C through 20, 25 and 30 to 34 °C.

Physically, this is Foucault's demonstration that eddy currents induced in a conductor moving through a magnetic field turn the mechanical work spent overcoming the magnetic drag into Joule heat. The experiment is now called 'Foucault's disc'; the currents are called Foucault currents.

Below is a supplementary order-of-magnitude illustration. It is mine, not Riemann's, and is not on the page:
- 150–200 rev/s corresponds to ω = 2π·150 ≈ 942 to 2π·200 ≈ 1257 rad/s.
- The total temperature rise is 18 K.
- For a thin disc of conductivity σ, thickness d and radius R in a uniform axial field B, the induced currents are purely azimuthal-free only in idealized geometries. In the standard textbook model of a disc spinning in a field confined to a region, the dissipation scales as P ∝ σ d B² ω² R⁴.

No derivation by Riemann is present. The note simply records experimental data, presumably as empirical input for his natural-philosophy speculations on electrodynamics and heat.
errors: No mathematical errors, since there is no computation. The final temperature is written 34 here, while the (illegible) next-page transcription ends with 33. This page clearly reads 34, which agrees with Foucault's reported rise from 16° to 34°. The next page may be a second copy of the same note, misread by the machine transcription or miscopied.

results.what: Record of Foucault's 1855 experiment: heating of a rotating bronze conductor between electromagnet poles (16 °C to 34 °C at 150–200 rev/s)
results.modern_name: Eddy-current (Foucault-current) heating; Foucault's disc; mechanical-to-thermal energy conversion via induction
results.usually_credited_to: Léon Foucault (1855), building on Arago's rotations (1824), Faraday's induction (1831) and Joule's work on heat from magneto-electric currents (1843)

deep.surprise_reason: This is an excerpt from a published 1855 journal report of a well-known experiment, with no original analysis by Riemann. It is of mild interest only as evidence of what Riemann was reading for his physical notes.

checkable.asserts: Total temperature rise recorded is 18 K
150–200 rev/s corresponds to angular velocities of about 942–1257 rad/s
The successive readings 16, 20, 25, 30, 34 are consistent, with total increase 18

transcription_corrections: 'mittelst eines ausgezeichneten[?] Räder' should probably read 'mittelst zweier eingreifender Räder' (by means of two meshing gears); the image shows 'eingrei-fenden Räder'.
'dessen Umdrehungsaxe eine gehärtete Welle bildet': the image seems to begin with 'Verlängerung' ('dessen Verlängerung eine gehärtete Welle bildet'), not 'Umdrehungsaxe'.
'{+einer+} Umdrehungsgeschwindigkeit': an inserted 'eine' appears to stand before 'Umdrehungsgeschwindigkeit'.
'[-Ein-] [-Thermometergefäß-]': the struck-out word is likely an earlier start; the intended reading is 'ein Thermometer, in seine Masse gesteckt'.
The initial phrase 'Ein massiver Bronzecylinder' is uncertain; a German word, possibly partly struck, precedes '(tore un tore en bronze)', with 'tore' struck out.
The year in 'Séance de l'ac. du 17 sept. 1855' is consistent with the image ('1855').
